title: Chapter 63 – The Garden Ledger
html:
[Lin Clan – Lin Wenyuan]

The trust has eleven clauses, and Wenyuan has read each of them eleven times.

He reads them again at the long table in the study, in the gray light of the first week of winter, with a brazier at his feet and a brush in his right hand. He has been holding the brush for an hour without writing anything. It is not for lack of ink. His hand has a way of forgetting what it is for, these days, and he has learned that if he holds a brush long enough, the fingers remember on their own.

One. The Garden shall remain the property of the Lin clan, held in trust by the Court for ten years.

Two. The Garden shall be surveyed by the Court's Garden Office in each season, and its yield recorded.

Three. No structure shall be built within the Orchard without the Office's leave.

Four. No part of the yield shall be sold beyond the clan, save through the Court's own buyers at the Court's own price.

He knows the rest by heart. Seven is the one he hates. Any discovery in the Garden of greater than ordinary import shall be reported to the Court within seven days. It has the shape of a clause written by someone who expects something to be found.

Ten years. In ten years Jian will be twenty. Lin Yue will be sixteen. Lin Hu will have finished his own Qi Refining and perhaps begun on the next road. Wenyuan will be forty-nine, and either a man who held the hill or a man who did not.

He puts down the brush.

Beside the trust lies Zhong's ledger.

It is the first one, a thin book bound in blue cloth, kept in the gatehouse by an old man who has no other work to do. Zhong delivered it himself this morning, with both hands, and stood in the doorway waiting while Wenyuan turned the pages. There are three weeks of entries. The date. The bed. The count of leaves, or roots, or stems. Who took what, and for whom, and why. Heartroot, bed nine, forty leaves, for Wenqing's ward, six children, fever. Frostbell, bed fourteen, three stems, for the guard Mao's widow, to be steeped. In Zhong's small, upright hand, the clan's whole winter is written down, and nothing in it is a lie.

The numbers are wrong.

They are not wrong by much. Wenyuan has spent twenty years learning to hear a figure that is a hair off true, as a musician hears a string. Bed nine's Heartroot, counted every ninth day, has given forty leaves for three weeks running. Before the autumn the beds gave forty-four. Frostbell, fourteen stems to a harvest, now thirteen. A tithe off the top, as if a thin hand had reached into every bed in the night and taken a little from each.

He turns back. He finds the date the figures begin to fall.

It is the night Jian went down to the terrace.

He knows it is, because Qinghe told him, two days after, in the dark, with her mouth against his shoulder. He went out in the third watch. Hu was on the steps. I did not follow. She has told him nothing else. She has not needed to. She has the careful stillness of a woman who has made a choice and means to keep it.

"It is a poor autumn, Elder Uncle," says Zhong, from the doorway. "I thought I should say. The beds are tired. Hu says the same."

"I have seen the numbers."

"They will recover by spring. I think." Zhong hesitates. "Or they will not. The beds do not say."

"No," says Wenyuan. "They do not."

He thanks the old man. Zhong bows, a little deeper than a man of seventy-one ought to, and leaves, and the study is quiet again except for the brazier's tick.

Wenyuan looks at the ledger for a long time.

A tenth, he thinks. A tenth of the Garden, taken in a single night. By my son.

He has not asked. He has decided, in the long hours since, that he will not. A boy of ten who can break a siege has earned the right to a locked door, and a father who loves him has no business with the key. But he is the Patriarch of a clan of three hundred and ninety-one, and a tenth of a winter's herbs is nineteen children's fevers, and he writes the number in the margin of the ledger in small neat characters, where nobody but himself will think to look.

Nine percent. Cause unknown.

It is the first lie he has put in a Lin ledger, and it is a small one, and he finds that his hand does not shake at all.

* * *

The council meets at noon in the east hall.

There are twenty-three seats, and nineteen are filled. Four are empty by death, two of them since the siege. Wenyuan sits in the Patriarch's chair, which is too wide for him and too old, and which creaked on the first day he sat in it as if it had been asked to carry something that was not a man.

"Tribute first," he says. "Wenjun."

Elder Aunt Wenjun does not stand. She is sixty-one, with an accountant's long fingers and an accountant's way of speaking in numbers, as if a figure were a kind of courtesy. "The autumn tribute is paid. Three hundred, in full, on the ninth day. The forty-two in arrears is cleared. We have two hundred and eighty-one low stones in the treasury and one middle stone, which I would prefer not to spend." She turns a page. "The Court's trust fee is a hundred a year. The first quarter is due at midwinter."

"A hundred," says someone, in a low voice. "On top of the tribute."

"On top of the tribute." Wenjun does not look up. "It is not a fee for the Garden. It is a fee for being watched."

Nobody laughs.

"Herb rules," says Wenyuan.

They have been written. They hang on the east wall of the hall, in Master Ji's best hand, and they are very simple. Herbs by need. The sick first, then children, then the Keepers, then everyone else. Nothing leaves the Orchard but through the ledger. Nothing is sold. Wenyuan watches the faces of the council as Wenqing reads them out, in her calm clinical voice, and sees what he expected: the old, careful relief of a people who have been hungry, and, behind it, in two or three of the faces, a quiet calculation.

"A tenth is a great deal of silver," says Elder Uncle Lin Ping, in his dry, slow way, "for a clan that has never had more than it could count."

"A tenth of what?" says Wenyuan.

"Of what we could sell, if we were allowed."

"We are not allowed."

"We are not allowed to sell to anyone but the Court," says Lin Ping. "The Court pays at the Court's price. Which is fair, I do not doubt. But the Court's price for Heartroot is eight stones a leaf. At Willow Ford, in the Pavilion, it is ten."

"The Court would take the rest," says Wenjun, flatly, "and ask where we got it."

It is the end of the matter. Ping bows his head, and subsides. He is not a bad man. He is a man who has done the sum, and who knows that somebody must.

They go on. The Keepers, Wenshi's guard, forty strong, drilled twice daily by Wenshi and by Hu in the quarry bowl, in a formation Hu calls the Funnel and Wenshi calls, with deep distaste, the Sieve. The Red Ridge tenants, two hundred families who held land of the Zhaos and now hold it of the Court, who come to the clan's wells and the clan's market and watch the Lin gate with careful eyes. Wenyuan listens. He asks a question. He makes a decision about a well, and a second about a debt, and a third, which he will regret, about a man's rent.

It is the work. It is, he thinks, not unlike drawing a talisman. One stroke at a time. A mistake in any one of them and the whole thing fails.

"One more thing," says Wenshi, from the foot of the table.

He is the captain of the Keepers, a thick, quiet man of thirty-six with a cracked rib that has healed crooked and a wrist that will never turn quite right. He has not spoken until now. He is looking at his own hands.

"Deputy Dou is at the gate," he says. "He has been there since the third bell. He asks for the Patriarch, alone."

* * *

They talk in the study, with the door shut and the brazier banked.

Dou has changed, in the week since the survey. He has put off the gray traveling robe for a black one with the Court's cloud-stitch at the collar, and he sits very straight, with his tally-stick across his knees and a thin case of oiled leather at his feet. He declines tea. He accepts water.

"I will be brief," he says. "I have been asked to ask you three things."

"Ask."

"The first." Dou takes a sheet of paper from the case, and lays it on the table between them, face up, with its edge squared to the edge of the wood. "The Arbiter has seen this. He has asked whether you have anything to add."

It is the sketch.

Wenyuan has not seen it. He had not known it would be so small, or so exact. Four lines, a thumb, a few tidy numbers. Palm 8.5 cm. Right. Child, under twelve. A faint shape drawn in a hand that is neither unkind nor warm, that knows only what it was told by the stone.

His own hand, on his knee, closes.

"Children play on the terrace," he says. "There are forty-one under twelve."

"Forty-one," says Dou. "Yes. I counted." He does not look up. "A silver print on a stone does not come from play, Patriarch. I have been in the Garden Office for nineteen years. I have seen the marks that Qi leaves. I have never seen a mark that stays. That one is not an accident."

"Then it is something the Garden did."

"A garden does not do things."

"This one does," says Wenyuan, and for a moment he thinks that he has said too much.

Dou writes a line. It is a short line. The pen does not hesitate.

"The second," he says. "The Garden. In the first notice, the Court was told it was a minor remnant. Eleven Wardens, some beds, a pool. The survey agrees. I am asked to confirm, in your own words, for the file: is it all? Is there anything in the Garden, or under it, beyond what the survey has recorded?"

Wenyuan looks at him.

It is a plain question, asked in a plain voice, by a man who has not been told what he is looking for. It is, he understands, the one question in the whole of the trust that cannot be answered by a clerk's count. It is also the only one that matters.

He thinks of a plate that opens for no one. He thinks of a boy of ten, coming in out of the dark with dust on his cloak. He thinks of Zhenshan, who counted forty steps every morning for forty years, and who never once asked what was at the bottom of them, because a man who holds a hill does not dig under it.

"The Garden," he says, "is what you have seen."

It is true. He has chosen every word.

Dou's pen stops. For the first time, he lifts his eyes. They are tired, intelligent, ledger-colored eyes, and they rest on Wenyuan's face for exactly as long as it would take to read a short line of script.

"Thank you," he says. He writes.

"And the third?"

"The third is not a question." Dou caps his brush. "It is a courtesy. In the fifth month, the Outer Court holds its Spring Register. Every child of an affiliated clan who is registered comes under the Court's eye, and is measured, in public, on the Mirror. Your son will be there. The Arbiter says that if there is a hand in this city that fits the sketch, the Register will be the place to find it." He folds the paper. "I think it is better you hear that from me than from a rumor."

It is not a threat. It is, if anything, the opposite. Wenyuan understands it, and understands who it is for, and feels something cold and grateful turn over in his chest.

"I thank you, Deputy."

"Do not." Dou rises, and bows exactly the required depth. "I have written that the Patriarch of the Lin clan was forthcoming and precise. I would be glad if that remained a fair description."

He leaves. The door closes. The brazier ticks.

Wenyuan sits for a long time, with his hand flat on the table, and the paper in front of him, where the deputy has left it.

Forthcoming and precise, he thinks.

He has lied to an officer of the Court, in his own house, in a voice he did not know he possessed. He has done it for a child. He would do it again. It does not make it clean. He takes the sketch and holds it over the brazier until the corner browns and lifts, and then, because there is a copy somewhere on a desk in the Outer Court and burning this one will change nothing, he takes it away from the flame. He folds it. He puts it in the drawer where he keeps the clan's old deeds.

I will keep it, he thinks. A man should not burn the evidence of his own choices.

* * *

Qinghe comes in after dark.

She does not knock. She has never knocked. She comes in with a lamp in one hand, and a thin sheaf of paper in the other, folded twice, and sets both on the table without a word. She has been out in the quarry bowl with the Keepers since noon, and there is rime on the hem of her cloak, and her hair has come down at one side.

"You spoke to the deputy," she says.

"I did."

"And?"

"I lied to him." He says it without softness. "By omission. I chose the words. He wrote them down."

She sits. She does not say it was necessary, or that she understands, or that it was not so bad. She pulls her chair a little closer and puts her cold hand over his, the one that does not shake, and they sit like that for as long as it takes the lamp to steady.

"I have been doing it for twenty years," she says. "Every road I walked, before you. It does not get lighter. It gets easier to carry." She turns his hand over. "It is a skill. Like drawing."

"I would rather not have it."

"I know." A faint, dry curl of the mouth. "That is why you will be good at it."

She pushes the sheaf across the table.

It is four pages, in her quick, slanting hand, written close and then ruled off in sections. He has not seen her write anything but a recipe in ten years. He picks up the first page.

For Jian. Read once. Burn.

1. Do not eat from a stranger's hand, or drink from his cup, before you have seen him eat. This is not about poison. It is about debt.

2. A Deacon's smile is a price. Ask what it costs before you accept it.

3. Learn who sits above whom. In a sect, a man's rank is his name. Bow to the rank, not the man, until you know which is which.

4. Never tell a healer a half-truth. They can hear it. Tell them a whole one that is not the one they were afraid of.

5. Sew two low stones into the hem of your short robe. Never spend them. They are the road home.

He reads on. There is a page on the Outer Affairs Hall and what its clerks are afraid of. There is a page on Elders, which says only: They have factions. You have none. This is both your danger and your freedom. There is a half-page on the courtyards, on who is likely to carry tales, and a list of three names in Qinghe's hand that he does not know and does not ask about. At the bottom of the last page, below a ruled line, she has written one more sentence, and crossed it out, and written it again.

You do not have to be the one who is always right.

He lowers the paper.

"He is ten," says Wenyuan.

"Yes."

"He is ten, and in seven months we will put him in a cart and send him to a place where no one has loved him for a day. They will put a mirror in front of him in a crowded hall and read him out loud." His voice has gone low. "I held him, Qinghe, the night of the siege. I could feel his heart through my sleeve. I did not know a body could hold so much and not break."

"He is not breaking."

"No. That is what frightens me."

She does not answer at once. The lamp has begun to gutter, and she trims the wick with two fingers, without looking, as she has done a thousand evenings.

"I asked him a question," she says, "in the autumn. After the siege. I asked him if he would go, if he could choose. He said he would stay and hold the hill." A pause. "And then he said that he could not hold it from here. That the hill was not the thing in danger. The hill was only where it was kept."

Wenyuan is silent.

"He is right," says Qinghe. "I do not know how he knows it. I have stopped asking. But whatever is coming, it is bigger than a clan, and it is not here, and he is the only one of us who can see the shape of it." Her hand tightens on his. "We can keep him on this hill until he is gray, Wenyuan, and it will not be safer. It will only be nearer."

Nearer, he thinks. To what?

He does not ask that either.

"Then he goes," he says.

"Then he goes."

"We write the list into him," says Wenyuan, "and we send him with every stone we can spare. And I will go to the Register, and sit in the back, and watch."

"You will not be let into the back."

"I will find a way."

She almost smiles. Then she is on her feet, and she has taken the lamp, and she is standing at the window with her hand pressed flat to the cold glass, looking out across the yard at the dark shape of the forge, where a single window is lit.

"He is not asleep," she says.

"No."

"He never is."

* * *

He goes to the forge at the third watch, because she is right and the window is lit.

Jian is sitting on an upturned crate with Pebble asleep across his knees and a half-built frame of spirit-iron wire on the bench in front of him. He has a small file in his hand. He is not filing. He looks up as the door opens, and Wenyuan sees at once that the boy has been awake for a day and a night, and that he has been doing sums.

"Father."

"I did not come to ask," says Wenyuan.

"I did not think you had."

He crosses the floor, and sits on the anvil stump across from the bench, with his bad hand in his lap. The forge is warm. It smells of oil and cold slag and the faint sweet smoke of the pine charcoal that Hu burns when he is thinking. On the far wall, in a row, the Keepers' spears stand in their rack like a stand of young trees.

"The beds are low," says Wenyuan.

Jian does not move. His face is a boy's face, narrow and tired, with the gold ring round the eyes that has not faded since the autumn. It does not change at all. It is only that he has stopped breathing for a moment, in the way a man does when he hears a footstep on a stair.

"Nine percent," says Wenyuan. "In the ledger. Since the night of the new moon. I have written it in the margin."

"Father..."

"I have written cause unknown." He keeps his voice level. "The Court's deputy asked me, three days ago, whether there was anything in the Garden beyond what he had counted. I told him there was not. I chose each word, and each word was true, and I would not have said any of them if I had not known that you could not. I want you to hear that from me." He turns his good hand over. "I am not telling you so that you will explain. I am telling you so that you will understand what it costs, and who is paying."

The file has gone still in Jian's fingers.

"I will make it up," he says, at last. His voice is very low. "The beds. I do not know how yet. But I will."

"I know."

"It was not for me. Or it was, but not only..." He stops. He starts again. "I cannot tell you what it was. I am sorry."

"You have said that," says Wenyuan, "many times, in many ways, since the autumn. It is not an apology I need." He reaches out, slowly, and sets his palm on the boy's head, over the stiff dark hair, where Zhenshan used to rest his, on the mornings when they counted the steps together. "I need you to eat. And sleep. And write to your mother. And when you are in that Court, and a man in a gray robe asks you a question you cannot answer, I need you to remember that there is a house behind you that has already decided what it will say."

Jian's eyes are bright. He does not blink.

"Yes, Father."

"Good." He takes his hand away. He does not trust his voice with anything more, and so he reaches into the breast of his tunic, and takes out a flat case of lacquered wood, and sets it on the bench between the wire frame and the file.

"Ten," he says. "Warding. The best I have drawn since the siege. They will not stop a Foundation blade, but they will make a man at Qi Refining nine think twice." He stands. "Do not use them for anything you could do with your head."

He is at the door when Jian speaks.

"Father."

He waits.

"The numbers in the ledger," says Jian. "When I put it right, I will tell you how."

"When it is safe," says Wenyuan, "you may tell me anything you like." He opens the door. The cold comes in, clean and sharp, smelling of snow. "Go to sleep."

* * *

The letter comes on the last day of the month, in a case sealed with a plain gray wax, borne by a Court courier who has ridden four days and looks it.

It is not from the Garden Office. It is not from the Arbiter. It is a short summons, in a clerk's flat hand, with the stamp of the Outer Court's Enforcement Hall at the foot, and it says that the matter of Zhao Bei, steward of Red Ridge, formerly of the Zhao family, shall be heard in open session at the Outer Court in the fifth month of the coming year, on the second day of the Spring Register, and that Lin Wenyuan, Patriarch of the Lin clan of Green Pine Hill, being the chief witness, is required to attend.

He reads it twice. He reads it a third time.

The date is the date of the Register.

He sits in the study with the paper in his hand and does not move. Outside, in the yard, a child is laughing. Lin Yue, probably. She has begun to laugh again in the evenings. It is a sound he has not wanted to hear in a long time, and has needed to.

I will be there, he thinks. I will be in the same hall, on the same day, under the same stamp.

He had been searching for a way to be in the back of the room. The Court has found one for him.

It is not a coincidence. He has lived too long with the Zhaos to believe it is. Someone, in an office he has never seen, has put a witness and a boy in the same building on the same morning, and has written it all out with the plain flat pen of a man who wishes it to look like an accident. He does not know why. He does not know whether it is a kindness or a trap.

He folds the letter along its creases. He puts it with the sketch, in the drawer with the old deeds.

Then he takes up his brush, and begins, very slowly, with a hand that remembers what it is for, to draw a Warding talisman. He draws it stroke by stroke, one line and then the next, as Zhenshan taught him, and he does not stop until the ink is dry and the hand is still.
